transcript:
# Day 18, Game Theory and Decisions: Coordination games and Schelling's focal points (Thomas Schelling, 1921 to 2016)

Picture this. You have to meet a stranger in New York City tomorrow. You know nothing about them. You cannot talk to them, text them, or leave a note. If you both show up at the same place at the same time, you each win. If you miss, you both lose. Where do you go, and when?

Thomas Schelling asked a room of students this in the 1950s. Most of them picked Grand Central Station, and nearly all of them picked noon. Nobody told them to. Nothing about Grand Central is logically better than Penn Station or the Empire State Building. But something about it stood out, and each person guessed that it would stand out to the other person too. That is the whole idea in one picture.

A coordination game is a situation where the players want the same thing, and the only hard part is landing on the same choice. Driving on the right or the left is the classic case. Nobody cares which side wins. Everybody cares that we all pick the same one. Compare that to the prisoner's dilemma from Day 8, where the players' interests pull against each other. In a coordination game the conflict is gone, but the problem is not. There are several outcomes that would all count as a Nash equilibrium (from Day 13, a set of choices where nobody can do better by changing alone), and the theory gives you no way to pick among them.

Schelling's answer was that real people solve this by finding a focal point: an option that stands out from the rest for some reason outside the formal game, so each player expects the other to notice it too. Noon stands out because it is the middle of the day. Grand Central stood out because it was the famous meeting spot. A focal point can come from tradition, from a round number, from a landmark, from fairness, from a prior agreement, or just from being the only option that is different. The key is not that it is better. The key is that it is obvious that it is obvious.

You see this everywhere once you know to look. Price negotiations tend to settle on round numbers or on splitting the difference, not because those are the right answers but because both sides can predict the other will accept them. Two business units that merge end up adopting the process that already had a name and a document. A military unit that loses radio contact falls back to the last briefed rally point, because everybody can guess that everybody else will. Cease fire lines settle on rivers. Schelling thought this was the quiet engine behind most of human coordination, including things like money, law and language.

Here is the strongest objection. Focal points are not predicted by the theory. They are read off from culture and psychology after the fact. A critic can say Schelling did not solve the problem of multiple equilibria, he just named it and pointed at where humans look for the answer. That is fair. Schelling admitted as much. His defense was that a theory of strategy that ignores how actual people coordinate is useless, and that focal points are real and often predictable if you know the shared background. Later experiments by Mehta, Starmer and Sugden in the 1990s backed this up: people do converge on salient options far more than chance, even with strangers. The weak spot remains that what counts as salient differs across cultures and groups, so a focal point that is obvious to your team may be invisible to your counterpart.

This builds straight on the last three readings in this track. Day 3 gave you players, strategies and payoffs. Day 8 showed what happens when interests collide. Day 13 showed that equilibrium can exist but still leave you stuck. Today is about how people actually get unstuck. It also links to the Strategy track, where Schelling will appear again as the thinker behind credible commitment and deterrence. The same man who studied where strangers meet also studied how nuclear powers avoid war, and the thread is the same: expectations about what the other side expects.

Question for the day: in your work, where is there a focal point that everyone silently defers to, and is it there because it is good or just because it is obvious?

Optional source: Thomas Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict (1960), chapter 3, "Bargaining, Communication, and Limited War," especially the section on tacit coordination.
